narrative:
The model predicted a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly 6th decile among accepted students) signaled that your academic performance had not reached the level typically needed to pass the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in the opposite direction. At 33.5 it is below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated this score as a mild positive signal that slightly increased the chance you might pass.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Like your third-year rank, being in the bottom decile (versus an average around 6th among accepted students) pulled the prediction back toward failure.

Taken together, the two weak academic rankings outweighed the modest lift from your LSAT, producing an overall risk of failure that the school was unwilling to accept.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your class standing in the remaining law school years, consider a structured bar-prep course that targets your specific weaknesses, and then retake the exam. A stronger academic record and a passing score will remove the main reasons for rejection and greatly improve your chances on reapplication. (248 words)
